title: A Token and Its Word: One Round Trip Through ItsDangerous
premise: A web app wants to hand a user's identity — `{"id": 5, "name": "itsdangerous"}` — to an untrusted place (a URL, a cookie, an email link) and get it back later without having stored anything server-side. The data must survive the trip in a form that is safe for URLs, and any tampering must be detectable on return. `URLSafeSerializer("secret key", "auth")` is the promise; this story follows the dict out to a token and back again, and notes exactly what that promise covers and what it does not.

chapters.title: The World the Dict Enters
chapters.data_in: secret_key='secret key', salt='auth', serializer=None, signer=None, signer_kwargs=None, fallback_signers=None
chapters.data_out: a URLSafeSerializer with secret_keys=[b'secret key'], salt=b'auth', serializer=_CompactJSON, is_text_serializer=True, signer=Signer, fallback_signers=[]
facts: A single `str` or `bytes` secret key is normalised into a one-element list by `_make_keys_list`; any other iterable becomes a list of keys, oldest to newest, which is the key-rotation feature.
`want_bytes` encodes text as UTF-8 with `errors='strict'`, so a secret key or salt is always compared as bytes, never as text.
`salt` defaults to `b"itsdangerous"`; passing `None` leaves it unset here so the Signer's own default applies later. The salt is not secret — it only separates signing contexts.
`URLSafeSerializerMixin` overrides `default_serializer` to `_CompactJSON`, which sets `separators=(",",":")` and `ensure_ascii=False`, producing shorter payloads than stdlib `json` defaults.

`is_text_serializer` decides text-vs-binary by actually calling `serializer.dumps({})` at construction time and checking for `str` — a probe, not a declaration; a custom serializer that raises on `{}` would fail at construction.
`fallback_signers` defaults to the class attribute `default_fallback_signers`, which is an empty list since 2.0 (the SHA-512 fallback was removed).
No signing or hashing happens here: `hashlib.sha1` is deliberately not touched at import or construction time (`_lazy_sha1`) so FIPS builds can reconfigure the default first.

open_questions.question: The salt 'auth' was merely turned into bytes and stored. Where does it actually enter the cryptography, and can it be confused with the secret?
A throwaway `dumps({})` was evaluated and remembered as `True`. What decision does that boolean control later?

chapters.title: Becoming a Payload
facts: The dict is serialised to the 30-byte text `{"id":5,"name":"itsdangerous"}` and then encoded to bytes; `dump_payload` always returns bytes even when the inner serializer returns text.
`serializer_kwargs` (empty here) are passed straight into `serializer.dumps`, so caller-supplied options affect the signed bytes.

The URL-safe mixin compresses every payload with zlib and keeps the compressed form only if it is shorter than `len(json) - 1`; for this 30-byte JSON it was not, so the original bytes were used and no marker byte was added.
`base64_encode` uses `base64.urlsafe_b64encode` and strips `=` padding, so the payload contains only `A-Za-z0-9-_` — safe in URLs and, importantly, free of the `.` separator.
Compression is applied to attacker-visible data before signing; the token's length leaks something about the payload's compressibility, which is a known (and accepted) property of this design.

open_questions.question: zlib ran and its output was thrown away. If it had been kept, how would the reader on the other side ever know to decompress?

chapters.title: A Signer Is Built for the Job
chapters.data_out: a fresh Signer(secret_keys=[b'secret key'], salt=b'auth', sep=b'.', key_derivation='django-concat', algorithm=HMACAlgorithm(_lazy_sha1))
facts: `make_signer(None)` substitutes the serializer's own salt, so `dumps`/`loads` without an explicit salt are guaranteed to use the same context key.
The whole `secret_keys` list is handed to the Signer, not just one key.

Road not taken: if `sep` were any ASCII letter, digit, `-`, `_` or `=` — characters that can appear inside a base64 signature — `Signer.__init__` raises `ValueError` immediately rather than producing ambiguous tokens. `b'.'` is not in `_base64_alphabet`, so construction proceeds.
`key_derivation` defaults to `'django-concat'` and `digest_method` to `_lazy_sha1`; a wrong `key_derivation` string is not rejected here — it raises `TypeError` only later, inside `derive_key`.
With no `algorithm` given, an `HMACAlgorithm` wrapping the digest method is constructed; a caller may substitute any `SigningAlgorithm`, including `NoneAlgorithm`, which signs nothing at all.
A new Signer object is created per `dumps` and per unsign attempt; signers hold no mutable per-message state.

open_questions.question: The signer received a list of keys but only one message to sign. Which key signs, and what is the list for?

chapters.title: The Signature, and the Token Leaves Home
facts: `derive_key(None)` uses `self.secret_keys[-1]` — the newest key signs — and under 'django-concat' computes `sha1(salt + b"signer" + secret_key).digest()`, here `sha1(b'authsignersecret key')`.
Derivation is a plain hash concatenation, not a KDF: the docstring states it is not a way to stretch a short password into a strong key, and short secret keys stay weak.
Because the salt is prefixed into the derived key, two serializers with the same secret key but different salts produce different signatures and cannot read each other's tokens.
The HMAC is computed over the base64 payload bytes with the derived key; the digest is then `base64_encode`d, giving the 27-character `6YP6T0BaO67XP--9UzTrmurXSmg`.
`sign` returns `value + sep + signature`, so the payload stays readable in the clear — this is integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality.
`dumps` decodes the signed bytes to `str` precisely because `is_text_serializer` was `True`; with a binary serializer the same code returns `bytes`.

open_questions.question: The dict is now travelling as readable base64 with a hash stuck on the end. What can the holder of the token learn, and what can they change?

answers.answer: The salt enters as a literal byte prefix in key derivation — `sha1(b'auth' + b'signer' + b'secret key')` — separating contexts without being secret itself.
`is_text_serializer=True` is what makes `dumps` return `rv.decode("utf-8")`, i.e. a `str` token instead of bytes.
Signing uses only the last (newest) key: `derive_key` defaults to `self.secret_keys[-1]`.

chapters.title: Back From the Untrusted World
chapters.data_out: bytes to verify, plus exactly one candidate Signer (salt=b'auth') from iter_unsigners
facts: `loads` accepts `str` or `bytes` and normalises with `want_bytes`; nothing about the token is trusted at this point.
`iter_unsigners` is a generator: it yields the primary signer first, then one signer per fallback configuration per secret key — so the current parameters are always tried before any legacy ones.
With `fallback_signers=[]` only one signer is produced here; fallbacks exist so digest methods or derivation schemes can be upgraded without invalidating tokens in the wild.
Each fallback entry may be a dict of kwargs, a `Signer` subclass, or a `(class, kwargs)` tuple — and, unlike the primary signer, fallbacks are constructed one key at a time, iterating `secret_keys`.

`loads` swallows `BadSignature` from each candidate and keeps only the last one; if every signer fails it re-raises that final exception, so the error a caller sees comes from the last signer tried, not necessarily the most informative one.
If `iter_unsigners` ever yielded nothing, `last_exception` would still be `None` and `raise None` would surface as a `TypeError` — reachable only by deliberately breaking the generator.

open_questions.question: Failures from each candidate signer are caught and discarded in a loop. What information does a rejected token carry with it, and does anything leak?

chapters.title: Splitting the Token Apart
chapters.data_out: value=b'eyJpZCI6NSwibmFtZSI6Iml0c2Rhbmdlcm91cyJ9' and raw sig bytes b'\xe9\x83\xfaO@Z;\xae\xd7?\xef\xbdS4\xeb\x9a\xea\xd7Jh' ready to compare
facts: Road not taken: a value with no `.` in it raises `BadSignature("No b'.' found in value")` before any crypto runs — and with no `payload` attached, so nothing tampered is offered back to the caller.

The split is `rsplit(sep, 1)`: the last dot wins, which is why the separator must not be a character that can occur in a base64 signature (enforced back in chapter 3) — payload dots, as used by the compression marker, are harmless.

`verify_signature` base64-decodes the presented signature inside a bare `except Exception: return False`, so malformed signature text becomes a plain verification failure rather than a `BadData` leak.
`base64_decode` re-pads the input and decodes with `errors='ignore'` on the ascii step, so junk characters are dropped rather than raising — verification of a garbled signature simply fails.

On mismatch, `unsign` raises `BadSignature(f"Signature {sig!r} does not match", payload=value)`: the unverified payload is deliberately attached so callers can inspect it, which is why `load_payload` is a separate, explicit step.

open_questions.question: Two byte strings now have to be judged equal. Is that comparison safe against an attacker who can time it, and is only one key consulted?

answers.answer: A rejected token comes back as `BadSignature` carrying the unverified `payload`; itsdangerous never decodes it for you in `loads` — `loads_unsafe`/`load_payload` make that choice explicit and unsafe by name.

chapters.title: The Verdict
chapters.data_in: key derivation for secret_key=b'secret key'; sig vs recomputed HMAC
facts: Verification loops over `reversed(self.secret_keys)`: newest key first, every key tried, returning `True` on the first match — this is what makes key rotation work, and it means an old key stays valid until it is removed from the list.
Here `derive_key` is called with an explicit key (`b'secret key'`), taking the `want_bytes` branch, and recomputes the same `sha1(b'authsignersecret key')` derived key as signing did.
The signature is recomputed from scratch and compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, a constant-time comparison, so the check does not leak the expected signature through timing.
A forged token must produce the right HMAC under one of the configured keys; without a key this is infeasible, which is the whole guarantee: tamper-evidence, not secrecy.
`SigningAlgorithm.verify_signature` is generic — a custom algorithm could verify asymmetrically, and `NoneAlgorithm` would accept an empty signature from anyone. The default is the safe one.
`Signer.validate` exists for callers who want a boolean instead of an exception; it swallows `BadSignature` only.

open_questions.question: The bytes handed back are still base64 and still look like a token. What turns them back into the caller's dict, and can that step itself be attacked?

answers.answer: Yes on both counts: `hmac.compare_digest` is constant-time, and `verify_signature` tries every key in `secret_keys` from newest to oldest before giving up.

chapters.title: Home Again, and What Was Promised
facts: A leading `b"."` is the compression marker: it is stripped and `zlib.decompress` is applied. This payload has none, matching chapter 2 where compression was discarded — the flag and the decision are two halves of the same contract.

Road not taken: a bad base64 body raises `BadPayload("Could not base64 decode the payload...")`, and a bad zlib body raises `BadPayload("Could not zlib decompress...")`, both keeping the original exception in `original_error`.

Because decompression happens only after a valid signature (when reached through `loads`), attacker-controlled zlib input is not processed unauthenticated on the happy path — but `load_payload` called directly on a `BadSignature.payload`, as the docs suggest for debugging, does decompress unverified data.

`Serializer.load_payload` decodes to UTF-8 text before calling `loads` because `is_text_serializer` was `True`, and wraps every exception from the inner serializer in `BadPayload` — so serializer mismatches surface as `BadData`, not arbitrary errors.

`BadPayload` is a `BadData` but *not* a `BadSignature`, so it escapes the retry loop in `loads` instead of causing the next signer to be tried: a valid signature over an unloadable payload fails loudly.

The round trip guarantees the returned object is the one that was dumped by a holder of one of the secret keys under this salt. It does not hide the data, does not expire it, and does not prevent replay — expiry needs `TimedSerializer`/`TimestampSigner`, and the default serializer being JSON (not pickle) is what keeps `load_payload` from being remote code execution.

answers.answer: A compressed payload is prefixed with `b"."`; `load_payload` strips that byte and calls `zlib.decompress`. No marker here, so the bytes were decoded as-is.
Everything: the holder can `base64_decode` the payload and read `{"id":5,...}` — nothing is encrypted. They cannot change it, because any edit invalidates the HMAC.
`load_payload` base64-decodes and JSON-parses the verified bytes; failures become `BadPayload` with the original error, and using JSON rather than pickle keeps this step from executing attacker data.
